item.title: Mangrove School + Makongo/Caterpillars w/ Q&A | For All the Children — Tue Oct 6, 7:00 PM — IU Cinema
item.description:
Mangrove School (Filipa César and Sónia Vaz Borges, Guinea Bissau, 2022): During the anticolonial struggle against Portuguese occupation, the free schools in Guinea Bissau moved deep into the jungle and found the mangroves. The schools were fashioned on the interwoven branches and roots. The directors film the mangroves as an infrastructure with a networked architecture, as the locus of transmission, of radical education, attentive to the memory of the struggles. The mangrove's branches are powerful and encourage networks, collectives, and horizontality. [35 min; documentary; Portuguese with English subtitles]
Makongo/Caterpillars (Elvis Sabin Ngaïbino, Central African Republic, 2020): Albert and André strive to create a school in their forest community in equatorial Central African Republic. As the only secondary school graduates in their village, they teach local children while relying on the annual makongo (caterpillar) harvest to fund their project. This vivid ethnographic portrai

item.title: One Person, No Vote: A lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson — Tue Oct 6, 7:00 PM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description:
One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression is Destroying Our Democracy, a lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson
Carol Anderson is the Robert W. Woodruff Professor of African American Studies at Emory University. She is the author of several bestselling books including: The Second: Race and Guns in a Fatally Unequal America (2020); One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy (2018), which was long-listed for the National Book Award in Non-Fiction; and the critically-acclaimed White Rage: The Unspoken Truth of our Racial Divide (2016), which won the 2016 National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism and was also a New York Times Bestseller, a New York Times Editor’s Pick, and listed on the Zora List of 100 Best Books by Black Woman Authors since 1850. item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Wed Oct 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Wed Oct 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Wed Oct 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: Paula Poundstone — Fri Oct 9, 7:00 PM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description:
Iconic comedian Paula Poundstone is known for her smart, observational humor and a spontaneous wit that has become the stuff of legend. She regularly plays theaters across the country, hosts a weekly comedy podcast, Nobody Listens to Paula Poundstone, and is a regular panelist on NPR’s Wait, Wait… Don’t Tell Me. She also voiced the character ‘Forgetter Paula’ in the feature films Inside Out and Inside Out 2.
Paula has starred in several HBO specials, including Cats, Cops and Stuff, which nabbed a cable ACE award for Best Comedy Special. She was the first female comic to host the White House Correspondents Dinner. She filmed live coverage of the 1992 Democratic and Republican National Conventions and the Presidential Inaugural for The Tonight Show with Jay Leno and at the 93rd Emmy Awards. Paula has starred in two television series, both entitled The Paula Poundstone Show.

Tickets go on sale August 11th!
The 8th Bloomington Boogies Concert features acclaimed musicians who play blues piano, boogie-woogie, stride and other jazz forms, and zydeco accordion. New artists include Jason Marsalis (vibes/drums), Deanna Bogart (piano/sax), Yoshi Z2 Tsuji, and special guest Silvan Zingg; returning favorites include Rob Rio, Sunpie Barnes (accordion) with Matt Hampsey (guitar) of Sunpie & the Louisiana Sunspots, and Dr. Keith McCutchen, plus the rhythm section: Gordon Bonham (guitar), Joe Donnelly (sax), Ron Kadish (bass), and Dan Hostetler (drums).
Bloomington Boogies has been voted a top 10 festival in Indiana. Its mission is to present world-class performers in Bloomington, and to introduce young people to artists and musical styles through public concerts and free educational activities, including school performances, workshops, and master classes. See a complete list of festival activities at https://bloomingtonboogies.com/home https://bloomingtonboogies.com/

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Mon Oct 12 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Mon Oct 12 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Mon Oct 12 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: Dine Out for the Library at Upland Brewing Company — Tue Oct 13, 11:00 AM — Upland Brewing Company
item.description:
Dine Out for the Library at Upland Brewing Company (350 W. 11th Street, Bloomington) every Tuesday in October from 11 AM–10 PM. A Bloomington staple for 27 years, Upland offers chef-crafted, seasonal menus featuring locally sourced ingredients, scratch-made recipes, and plenty of creative options for vegetarians—all reflecting the same artisan spirit found in their beers. Enjoy inside dining or cozy up on their patio where both children and canine friends are welcome. Show your flyer and Upland will donate 20% of your bill to the Friends of the Library to help make amazing Library programs possible. Flyers available at the Friends Bookstore, all Monroe County Public Library branches and online at mcpl.info/dineout
Source: Limestone Post, WFHB Community Calendar

item.title: Fall 2026 CLACS Faculty Research Symposium with Luis A. González — Tue Oct 13, 4:00 PM — Hamilton Lugar School
item.description: CLACS Faculty Research Symposium welcomes Luis A. González, Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University as he presents: Books in Formerly Sacred Spaces: The Story of a Public Library, a President, and an Artist — Jiquilpan, Mexico, 1941 Abstract: This presentation considers the Gabino Ortiz Public Library, notably founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in his hometown of Jiquilpan, Michoacán, in 1941. As part of his national cultural project, President Cárdenas opened the library within a repurposed church which also houses murals by José Clemente Orozco depicting events from the Mexican Revolution. This case study presents a compelling opportunity to examine the intersections of state cultural policy, collective memory, and the social imaginary of the library in modern Mexico.
